content.intro: In this lesson, you will explore namespaces and attributes within XML Namespaces. You will connect its syllabus topics to an inspectable example, check the expected result, and note tool/version limits.
content.why_it_matters: Namespaces and Attributes matters because XML workflows rely on explicit structure and predictable processing. The lesson helps you reason about unprefixed attributes, avoid a common misunderstanding, and make a result reproducible for another developer.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: An XML namespace is identified by its namespace name (commonly a URI). A prefix is a local alias bound by xmlns; the prefix spelling is not the identity. An unprefixed attribute does not inherit the default element namespace.

content_blocks.title: Connect the subtopics
content_blocks.text: This lesson explicitly covers: Unprefixed attributes; Namespace-qualified attributes; Default namespace behavior; Avoiding namespace misunderstandings. Treat these as connected parts of one workflow: define the structure, make the relevant assumptions explicit, and verify a result with a small known input.

content_blocks.title: Inspectable example: Namespaces and Attributes
content_blocks.expected_output: The two item elements use different namespace names even though both local names are item. Prefix spelling is only an alias for the namespace URI.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Inspect this example as text. Run it only in a processor that supports the shown language/version; the standard CodeLeaf playground previews HTML/CSS/JavaScript only and does not execute XML, XSD, XPath, XSLT, XQuery, Python, or SQL. When querying namespaced XML, bind a prefix in the XPath/XSLT host context and use that prefix in expressions. Two prefixes bound to the same namespace URI refer to the same expanded names.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a document is correct because it looks readable.
common_mistakes.why: Visual appearance does not prove well-formedness, schema validity, correct namespace handling, or application-level meaning.
common_mistakes.fix: Parse and validate the document with the intended processor, then assert its meaning using a focused test.

common_mistakes.problem: Mixing specification features with processor support.
common_mistakes.why: A standard may define features that a specific runtime does not implement.
common_mistakes.fix: Record the version and feature support; test with the actual target processor.

common_mistakes.why: Missing values, wrong types, namespace differences, or boundary inputs can expose failures.
common_mistakes.fix: Add a valid case, an invalid case, and an edge case to the verification notes.
